title: Insurance Explained
text:
Definitions
Insurance (CPI). The ABS price index for comparable home building, home contents, motor vehicle and compulsory third party (CTP) insurance policies. It measures price change, not what households spend in total. It does not include health insurance, which the ABS classifies in the Health group.
Insurance and financial services (CPI group). A broader group that also includes deposit and loan fees and other financial services. It is not the same as insurance.
Gross written premiums (APRA). Total premium revenue written by insurers. It grows with the number of policies and the value insured, as well as with prices, so it is not a measure of price inflation.
Affordability stress (Actuaries Institute). A home insurance premium above four weeks of gross household income.
Underinsurance. Cover that would not pay the full cost of rebuilding or replacing what is insured. Different from affordability stress and from having no insurance.

title: What can consumers do about rising premiums?
text: This page gives general information. It is not financial product advice and does not take your circumstances into account. It does not recommend any insurer or product.

title: What can consumers do about rising premiums?
text:
Renewals
In ASIC’s research on car insurance, 67% of consumers renewed with the same insurer, and 40% neither contacted their insurer nor compared quotes. Of those who did contact their insurer, 31% obtained a lower premium without changing their cover (ASIC 2026).
ASIC found that no insurer in its review explained the key factors behind a premium in quote and renewal documents. It expects insurers to explain the main factors behind a customer’s premium and why it changed (ASIC 2026).

title: What can consumers do about rising premiums?
text:
Payment method
ASIC found that paying car insurance by instalments often cost 10% to 20% more than paying annually, and that 54% of consumers either did not know this or missed it (ASIC 2026).

title: What can consumers do about rising premiums?
text:
Excess
The excess is the amount the policyholder pays towards each claim. A higher excess usually lowers the premium and increases the amount paid when a claim is made.

title: What can consumers do about rising premiums?
text:
Sum insured
Home building cover pays up to the sum insured on the policy. ABS prices for new dwellings rose 41.3% over the five years to the September quarter 2026.

title: What can consumers do about rising premiums?
text:
Mitigation
The ACCC found that more insurers now recognise steps policyholders take to reduce the risk of cyclone damage, but some have yet to put a framework in place and the information they give consumers varies in clarity (ACCC 2026).

title: What can consumers do about rising premiums?
text:
Where to get help

Free financial counselling. The National Debt Helpline offers free, confidential help from financial counsellors.
Complaints. The Australian Financial Complaints Authority is a free, independent dispute resolution service.
Information. ASIC’s Moneysmart has independent guidance on choosing and comparing insurance.


Last reviewed 3 November 2026.

title: Why are insurance premiums increasing in Australia?
text:
Short answer
Insurance prices in Australia rose 47.0% over the five years to the September quarter 2026, compared with 24.6% for overall consumer prices.
Regulators and industry bodies report higher claims costs, large natural disaster losses and higher reinsurance costs as pressures on premiums.

title: Why are insurance premiums increasing in Australia?
text:
How much have premiums risen?
The ABS insurance price index rose 5.4% in the year to September 2026, against 4.3% for the all-groups CPI. Over five years, insurance prices rose 47.0% and all goods and services 24.6% (Insurance trends).
Figures for specific products come from different sources and measure different things.

Car insurance. ASIC reports that motor vehicle premiums grew by more than 42% between 2019 and 2024, and by a further 8% in the 12 months to July 2025 (ASIC 2026).
Home and contents insurance. The ACCC found that average home and contents premiums outside northern Australia rose 18% in 2023–24 (ACCC 2025), and a further 10%, to $2,310, in 2024–25 (ACCC 2026).

The ABS index tracks the price of comparable policies. Average premiums also change when people insure more valuable homes or change their cover, so the two are not directly comparable.

title: Why are insurance premiums increasing in Australia?
text:
What goes into a premium?
Actuaries start from a technical premium:

Technical premium = expected claims + expenses + risk and capital loading

Expected claims depend on how often claims happen and how much each one costs. Expenses are operating costs (administration, marketing and claims handling) and commissions paid to intermediaries. The risk and capital loading covers reinsurance and a margin for profit or return on capital (ACCC 2020, 60–61).
Insurers then adjust the technical premium for competitive or market positioning, or to manage their exposure. These adjustments are not directly related to the risk of the property. Discounts, surcharges for options such as monthly payment, taxes, duties and levies are applied last, giving the price the customer pays (ACCC 2020, 60–61).

title: Why are insurance premiums increasing in Australia?
section: What regulators and industry bodies report
text:
What regulators and industry bodies report

Claims costs
ABS prices for new dwellings rose 41.3% over the five years to the September quarter 2026, and prices for vehicle maintenance and repair rose 27.4%. Insurers told the ACCC that building material and labour cost inflation is one of the factors behind high premiums (ACCC 2025). The ACCC’s final report found that claims cost inflation and extreme weather events are pushing premiums higher across Australia (ACCC 2026).


Natural disasters
The Insurance Council of Australia reported $7.17 billion in insured losses from more than 300,000 claims across the 2022 flood events (Insurance Council of Australia 2023). See How do natural disasters affect insurance premiums?


Reinsurance
The Actuaries Institute found that home insurance premium increases in the year to March 2024 were primarily a consequence of higher reinsurance costs during 2023 (Actuaries Institute 2024).
After insurers joined the government-backed cyclone reinsurance pool, the ACCC found that average home insurance premiums per $100,000 sum insured in higher cyclone risk areas fell by 11% in the first year. In areas with no cyclone risk they rose 6%. Up to two years after insurers joined, premiums in higher-risk areas were 14% below pre-pool levels. Insurers are passing on the lower reinsurance rates to policyholders in higher cyclone risk areas (ACCC 2026).


Capital, taxes and levies
Insurers must hold capital against the risk of large losses, and the cost of that capital is part of the cost of insurance. Insurers also pay expenses, commissions, taxes and levies, and often pass these costs on to policyholders (Huang 2024).


Competition and pricing strategy
ASIC found that 31% of car insurance customers who contacted their insurer about a renewal obtained a lower premium without changing their cover (ASIC 2026). Pricing that takes account of how likely a customer is to shop around, known as price optimisation, is legal in Australia (Huang 2024).


Data and risk modelling
The ACCC’s Northern Australia Insurance Inquiry found that better access to data, and more sophisticated analysis of it, has enabled insurers in northern Australia to price risk at an individual address level, not at a postcode or regional level, particularly for cyclone and flood risk. This has resulted in very large premium increases for some customers, while lower-risk customers may have seen reductions (ACCC 2020, ix). In one case, an insurer’s move to address-level cyclone pricing raised one customer’s premium by 70%, from about $3,000 to $5,000, and lowered another’s by 21%, from about $1,900 to $1,500 (ACCC 2020, 65).
With AI and big data, insurers can estimate the risk of each property more accurately. This more individualised pricing can lead to higher premiums for properties with higher risk levels (Huang 2024).

ABS figures: ABS, Consumer Price Index, Australia (Data API, dataflow CPI), original series, retrieved 3 November 2026. Last reviewed 3 November 2026.

title: How does insurance contribute to inflation?
text:
Short answer
Insurance makes up 1.36% of the Consumer Price Index basket. In the year to September 2026, insurance prices rose 5.4% and added 0.07 percentage points to the 4.3% rise in the CPI.

title: How does insurance contribute to inflation?
text:
How the CPI measures insurance
The CPI combines two pieces of information for each item: how much its price changed, and its weight in household spending.
Price. The insurance expenditure class covers comprehensive insurance for dwellings, home contents and motor vehicles, and compulsory third party motor vehicle insurance. Health insurance is classified in the Health group. The ABS measures price change using gross premiums, collected each month from web-scraped price quotes for a range of customer profiles. The index measures price change, not what households spend in total, and the ABS does not publish separate indexes for home and car insurance (ABS 2025).
Weight. The CPI weights insurance by the cost of the service provided by insurers, which the ABS measures as gross premiums less claims, rather than by the gross premiums households pay. The ABS updates the weights once a year, using National Accounts data, and holds them fixed between updates (ABS 2025).

title: How does insurance contribute to inflation?
section: How much insurance adds to inflation
text:
How much insurance adds to inflation
At the December quarter 2024 reweighting, insurance accounted for 1.36% of the all-groups CPI. In the year to September 2026, it contributed 0.07 percentage points of the 4.3% annual rise (ABS 2026a).

title: How does insurance contribute to inflation?
text:
The Selected Living Cost Indexes
The ABS’s Selected Living Cost Indexes weight insurance by the gross premiums households pay, rather than the net value used in the CPI (ABS 2026b).

title: How does insurance contribute to inflation?
text:
Taxes on premiums
When the GST was introduced in 2000, the CPI insurance index rose about 30% in a year, much more than the premiums households paid. Taxes are charged on gross premiums but were measured against the smaller net base used in the CPI (ABS 2000).

Last reviewed 3 November 2026.

title: Insurance Explained
text:
Why this site exists
Insurance costs have become a major part of the cost-of-living debate in Australia. Useful information is published by the Australian Bureau of Statistics, APRA, ASIC, the ACCC, the Reserve Bank, the Actuaries Institute and others. Each serves a different purpose, and their measures are easy to misread when combined.
Insurance Explained brings these sources into one place and explains what each one measures. It helps answer four questions:

What is happening? How insurance prices, claims, risks and affordability are changing.
Why is it happening? Which explanations are supported by evidence, and how strongly.
Why does it matter? The consequences for households, insurers, policymakers and society.
What can be done? Practical steps for consumers, and options for insurers, regulators and governments.

title: Insurance Explained
text:
Academic leadership
Fei Huang is Associate Professor of Risk and Actuarial Studies at UNSW Business School, UNSW Sydney. Her research covers insurance pricing, responsible AI, algorithmic fairness, and the fairness and resilience of insurance markets under technological and climate change. She co-founded and co-leads the AI4Insurance Lab, which works on responsible AI for insurance with industry and government.

title: How do natural disasters affect insurance premiums?
text:
Short answer
Insurers estimate the expected cost of claims from each natural peril separately, such as flood, cyclone, bushfire and storm, and build it into each property’s premium according to its relative risk. In 2024–25 the average home and contents premium was almost $5,000 in north Western Australia, compared with $2,310 outside northern Australia.

title: How do natural disasters affect insurance premiums?
section: How insurers price natural hazard risk
text:
How insurers price natural hazard risk
Insurers split expected claims into working claims, such as theft, glass and water damage, and natural peril claims. They generally model each peril separately, estimating how often claims occur and how much each one costs. The models for natural perils are generally developed by industry specialists or reinsurers and supplemented with insurers’ own claims data. Some insurers estimate the average annual loss for a peril across their portfolio and allocate it to policies by relative risk. Others build up the expected cost policy by policy (ACCC 2020, 62).
These models combine:

Hazard. How likely and how severe floods, bushfires, cyclones and storms are at that location.
Exposure. What is at risk: the building, its contents, and their value.
Vulnerability. How much damage a given event would cause, which depends on construction, elevation and other features.

Insurers also buy reinsurance to cover very large losses, and hold capital to pay claims after a very bad year. Insurers pass higher reinsurance costs on to consumers, and the cost of capital is part of the cost of insurance (Huang 2024).

title: How do natural disasters affect insurance premiums?
text:
Premiums in high-risk areas
The ACCC found that in 2024–25 the average home and contents premium was almost $5,000 a year in north Western Australia, over $3,500 in the Northern Territory and more than $3,100 in north Queensland. Outside northern Australia it was $2,310 (ACCC 2026).

title: How do natural disasters affect insurance premiums?
text:
Recent disaster losses
The Insurance Council of Australia reported $7.17 billion in insured losses from more than 300,000 claims across the 2022 flood events (Insurance Council of Australia 2023).

title: How do natural disasters affect insurance premiums?
text:
Reinsurance and the cyclone pool
The Actuaries Institute found that home insurance premium increases in the year to March 2024 were primarily a consequence of higher reinsurance costs during 2023 (Actuaries Institute 2024).
The Australian Government set up a cyclone reinsurance pool, run by the Australian Reinsurance Pool Corporation, from 1 July 2022. It is backed by a $10 billion government guarantee and covers cyclone and related flood risk for home, contents, strata and small business policies (ARPC 2026).
After insurers joined the pool, the ACCC found that average home insurance premiums per $100,000 sum insured in higher cyclone risk areas fell 11% in the first year. In areas with no cyclone risk they rose 6%. Up to two years after insurers joined, premiums in higher-risk areas were 14% below pre-pool levels. Insurers are passing on the lower reinsurance rates to policyholders in higher cyclone risk areas. More insurers now recognise mitigation by policyholders, but some have yet to put a framework in place (ACCC 2026).

title: How do natural disasters affect insurance premiums?
text:
Climate change
Australia’s climate has warmed by 1.51 ± 0.23 °C since national records began in 1910. CSIRO and the Bureau of Meteorology report an increase in extreme fire weather and a longer fire season across large parts of the country since the 1950s. Heavy short-term rainfall events are becoming more intense (CSIRO and Bureau of Meteorology 2024).
APRA’s 2026 climate stress test found that, under a scenario with higher physical risks, expected annual losses from weather-related events could rise from around $7 billion today to more than $16 billion by 2050. APRA states that this is a stress scenario, not a forecast (APRA 2026).

Last reviewed 3 November 2026.

title: Why are some households underinsured or uninsured?
text:
Short answer
A household is underinsured when its cover would not pay the full cost of rebuilding or replacing what it owns. It is uninsured when it has no cover at all.
APRA estimates that around one in seven Australian houses are uninsured today. About half of households surveyed by the ACCC rated their home insurance as unaffordable or barely affordable.

title: Why are some households underinsured or uninsured?
text:
What the estimates show
Affordability stress. The Actuaries Institute estimates that 15% of Australian households, or 1.61 million, were in home insurance affordability stress in the year to March 2024, up from 12% a year earlier. It defines stress as a home insurance premium above four weeks of gross household income (Actuaries Institute 2024).
How households rate the cost. In a survey commissioned for its final insurance monitoring report, the ACCC found that around half of the households surveyed across Australia rated their home insurance as unaffordable or barely affordable, regardless of the cyclone risk they face (ACCC 2026).
Non-insurance. APRA estimates that around one in seven Australian houses are uninsured today. The estimate comes from APRA’s climate stress test, carried out with five large insurers that together write around 80% of home insurance by gross written premium (APRA 2026).
The Australia Institute estimates that in 2023, 344,523 Australian households had no home building insurance and 533,229 were underinsured, about 1 in 30 and 1 in 20 households (Thrower 2025). Its estimate counts households and APRA’s counts houses, and the two use different data and definitions.
Projections. Under both of APRA’s climate stress scenarios, the share of uninsured houses could rise to around one in four by 2050. That is about one million more homes without adequate insurance. The protection gap could exceed 40% in rural areas. APRA states that these are stress scenarios, not forecasts (APRA 2026).

title: Why are some households underinsured or uninsured?
text:
Reported reasons
The ACCC reported hearing that households and small businesses were increasing their excesses and reducing their cover in response to high premiums (ACCC 2025).
Home building cover pays up to the sum insured on the policy. ABS prices for new dwellings rose 41.3% over the five years to the September quarter 2026.

title: Why are some households underinsured or uninsured?
text:
Consequences
APRA notes that when homes are uninsured or underinsured, losses are more likely to be borne by households, banks or government, which increases risks to the financial system (APRA 2026).

Last reviewed 3 November 2026.

title: Insurance Explained
text:
About these figures


What the insurance index measures
The CPI insurance expenditure class covers comprehensive insurance for dwellings, home contents and motor vehicles, and compulsory third party motor vehicle insurance. Health insurance is not included. The ABS classifies it in the Health group, under Medical and hospital services.1


Insurance, or insurance and financial services?
“Insurance” is an expenditure class, the lowest level at which the ABS publishes price indexes. “Insurance and financial services” is a broader CPI group that adds deposit and loan fees and other financial services. The two measure different things.


The 2000 spike
The insurance index rose by about 30% in the year to June 2000. The ABS attributed this mainly to the GST. Under the method used then, the CPI valued insurance as the net service households receive, roughly premiums less claims. Taxes on premiums are a larger share of that smaller base, so the GST moved the index by more than it moved the premiums households paid.2


Monthly and quarterly figures
Since November 2025 the ABS has published a complete monthly CPI. The quarterly CPI is the average of the three months in each quarter. This page uses ABS-published monthly annual changes for the headline figure and quarterly index numbers for long-run history.
